item.title: Re: Love at Long Last
item.content:encoded:
(Can't give greenlights)

To start off, I really really like this narrative. Dear Nia is a really great story with themes and technology that would be right at home in the foundation universe. Of course, as has already been noted, the main focus in writing will need to be on changing certain aspects of the story so that it can't be considered plagiarism.

+ Show crit
- Begone crit

…the primary one being that Chase's universe orbits a Red Dwarf while Underwood's earth (our Earth) orbits a Yellow dwarf.

While this does present some really cool imagery, it might need some minor explanation in the article, as the earth would be a very different place if it were orbiting a red dwarf. Orbiting a different class of star but still resulting in nearly identical timelines is a bit of a stretch beyond the multiverse theory. If you wanted to keep Chase's sun a Red Dwarf, perhaps you could explain by saying the mass of the sun was changed due to advance foundation testing or anomalies in that dimension? Ultimately though, this is only likely to be noticed by astro and quantum physics nerds like me and won't detract from the narrative.

This leads to an event known as "Gothic Storm", the first known Reality-Merging Class Scenario (RMK-Class) in that reality. The aftermath is chaotic, and leads to public awareness of the Foundation, the release of numerous anomalies, and shifts of entire galaxies in the universe.

I really like these consequences, as it does something the original story doesn't: showing the direct consequences of not letting go. However, since reality ending scenarios don't carry much weight in a narrative like this, perhaps also having a more personal consequence could give the narrative more of a punch. Perhaps either Underwood or Chase has a child, but due to Underwood's persistence in contacting Chase, the collapsing realities causes the death of the child. This gives us a more emotional and relatable consequence to Underwood not being able to let go and could show her that her actions have only caused more suffering to those she has left. This would also help set this story apart from Dear Nia.

Dr. Underwood had seemingly disappeared, while Dr. Chase was discovered in her office. The document ends with an interview with Chase, and remains the only documentation of this event.

While this does give the narrative some mystery and a feeling of being unresolved, it feels a bit out of place. IMO, Underwood should not disappear, or at least be allowed to at least give a final log or message that shows us whether she's realized the weight and consequences of her actions or not. This could help wrap up the story's theme and transition better into the interview with Chase.

With a few minor tweaks, I would definitely give this a greenlight if I could.

item.title: Re: Accessible Issue
item.content:encoded:
Hey ResearcherRando, thanks for bringing these issues up. If we could get some clarification on one of your points, that'd be great.

+ Snipped for mobile users
– hide block

I think the ability for more freedom in trying to convey what makes an idea worth it could benefit this site greatly. Once again: this spot isn’t impossible, but cam present real problems to someone in trying to cram an idea into a small format.

What are you suggesting we change, specifically? That we raise the word count limit on idea posts? Authors have a number of resources at their disposal already to receive crit which aren't encumbered by a word limit, whether that's the IRC chatrooms, a couple trusted Discord servers, or other avenues.1 Moreover the greenlighting process isn't mandatory for posting to the site — it's only a requirement in order to use the draft forum.

With that said, authors seems pretty free to mix and match what styles of critique work for them.

For a site requiring hard work from new creators, all it takes is ten people deciding to press a button saying they didn’t like it, and that says to the author this page is worthy of deletion.

Bit of a correction here: the -10 deletion threshold means that ten more people downvote the page than upvote it, not that ten people overall downvote.

in trying to add to something I’ve seen as fun and a little silly, I’ve been met with an incredibly high wall, in some ways earned by the site, but in many ways just as ridiculous.

I agree, it takes a lot of work to get something to stick on this site. If you're driven to see your idea(s) succeed, we encourage you to continue working on them up-until-and-beyond the point that they'll stay on the site. This site's high standards are meant as less of an impassible boundary and more as a motivator.

Footnotes
1. The word limit was initially put in place at the request of critters — before it was implemented, ideas tended to be exceedingly long and directionless. The rule intends to force new authors to streamline their ideas and make them look more appealing to critters (moreso than giant walls of text, anyways). Personally I think 400 words is rather generous.

item.title: Festive Jello Strikes Back (1st SCP idea)
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre (Optional): Mystery, Horror

Elevator Pitch: A seemingly innocent plate of Christmas gelatin (Festive season!), through further analysis, has been determined to be a cognitohazard employed by a gelatinous anomaly. It is able to detect prey by secreting pheromones into the air that when inhaled, awakens a predatory instinct within the gelatinous mass to envelop and consume affected prey item within a 5-meter radius of the plate.

Central Narrative: Field Agents dispatched to investigate an unexplained suburban disappearance of an entire family fails to report to Command. Ergo, an MTF team is deployed to follow up the disappearance, discovering human remains contained inside a mass of layered Christmas jello of an unknown origin. The object is retrieved and returned to an SCP Site wherein it is contained and the Foundation proceeds to conduct testing on the anomaly and gain additional understanding of its anomalous properties for optimal containment procedures.

After the SCP is confirmed a cognitohazard, it is suspected that the SCP was manufactured by a hitherto unknown Group of Interest. The Foundation launches a wider investigation into the origin of the SCP, sending Field Agents to return to the abandoned suburban home where it was originally discovered. The exploration log indicates that the agent discovers the original packaging and after finding out the brand name, another subsequent investigation reveals the identity of the Group of Interest that managed to evade Foundation radar up to this incident. The story ends with a footnote that ongoing surveillance and monitoring of the G.O.I is underway in order to assess the threat level of the parent G.O.I and ultimately deem whether Foundation intervention is necessary.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: The hook starts with the mysterious disappearance of Foundation Field Agents in a peaceful suburban area with no record of kidnapping, homicides or break and entry crimes. This leads to the discovery of the SCP (Through an exploration log). Then the SCP Foundation attempts to understand the SCP's unknown properties (Experimentation log), allowing effective containment to be achieved. The SCP Foundation reasons from its nature as a cognitohazard that there was a strong possibility that the SCP was artificially engineered. The audience is constantly kept engaged by a linear narrative starting off with mystery that later unfolds into a deeper investigation of the SCP's origins.

Additional Notes: Have yet to determine a name for the G.O.I responsible for the manufacturing of the SCP, and have not yet decided whether the G.O.I are a belligerent or benevolent organisation.


Forum category: Writing Help / Help: Ideas Critique
Forum thread: Festive Jello Strikes Back

The larger problem with that particular div is, however, that its contents don't justify the space it takes up on the page.

item.title: Re: My SCP idea
item.content:encoded:
It's a pretty simple concept. There's nothing wrong simplicity per se, but the simpler your idea, the more the article will need to be carried by the quality of the execution. The success of an article like this will depend pretty much entirely on your ability to create an atmosphere that draws the reader in and creates a sense of dread.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: High danger level and unic containiment procedures recommending you to poison yourself to avoid the anomaly

In fiction, something being "dangerous" does not necessarily make it scary or interesting to the reader. Honestly, my attention isn't being grabbed by this, and the way you relied so strongly on a movie scene to convey your idea doesn't inspire my confidence in your ability execute this concept at the level of skill it requires. I understand that the language barrier might be an issue, though, so I won't hold it against you.

we read a letter by the apartment past owner that tells us it’s backstory…

This sounds pretty significant to the story, so it's strange that you've mentioned it as an afterthought here. What does the backstory tell us about the anomaly? How does it enhance the mood you want to convey? You're seeking a greenlight, but I can't evaluate your ideas properly if you haven't thought them through yet.

Overall it sounds like you have a pretty long article in mind, supported by some very broad ideas. That's doesn't mean you're doomed to fail by default, but it does present some rather sizeable challenges for you. If you decide to proceed, my advice for your next step is that you create a (reasonably) detailed outline for how you intend the article to flow from start to finish.

item.title: Re: SCP Idea - Algernon-13
item.content:encoded:
I like the idea of there being a mysterious star exerting influence over humans, and then gradually learning that the star is intelligent and acting deliberately to some terrible end. On the other hand, the "Algernoning" effect you described doesn't really interest me at all. I think part of the reason is that the Algernonification is tied to the victims' respective professions in such a straightforward way. There's no intrigue when the outcome of an experiment is so predictable, and there's no impact in inflicting misery on a series of characters without having some degree of emotional buildup and payoff.

No greenlight from me I'm afraid, but I think the idea is worth revisiting and revising.

1) Why is The Foundation the only one being affected? Why not members of other groups? Heck, why not other individuals? And keep in mind that there are people giving birth, suffering from imminent death, and any number of other medical conditions. And I'm not even really getting into accidents or the possibility of the effects of sex or other issues.

It's a great idea but there are a lot of questions here.

item.title: Re: My first SCP; The Corn Monkeys
item.content:encoded:
1) As cybersqyd noted, you have too much going on. The key is to keep it simple; only add in things that add to it and figure out when too much is too much. The special diet makes no sense: Corn and blood are all there is to eat and it's unlikely that anyone will be able to force the monkey to eat anything else. The child's scream doesn't really add anything to it either, so that could be dropped. Just look for stuff that adds too much and go down the list looking for stuff that looks cool but doesn't really add to it.

On the flip side: They're small critters with high metabolism in an area that suffers really cold winters. Given the small size of their territory, are they getting enough to eat, and what happens when winter happens? Just something to consider.

2) The Hook section needs to show why we care about it, not be used for further description. We need to know what purpose it serves, be it a niche, a symbolic purpose, or just making it a point. It's a monkey in the middle of a field; why should we care? This is where you give us a reason to care and show how it fits into the SCP-U as a whole.

3) For future reference, you shouldn't be showing a sandbox page without being asked. That said, if it can only live in a three-acre section then a fence is all you need and that mostly to keep others out. Also, they have some sapience; that they are using spines as decoration shows some intelligence. Why not use them to harvest the field instead of sending the family in, with the monkeys keeping what they need.

This eliminates the need for them to be nice to the family while showing that they are aware of their precarious status. They still wouldn't molest the family for basically farming, but that keeps their territory to them.

Also, I'd point out that they are technically "Safe"; they are isolated, they are limited to that area, and only if you go into their territory are there problems.

Overall, great idea but needs some editing.

item.title: Re: Last Flight Out (SEEKING GREENLIGHT)
item.content:encoded:
I'll also note that, while those things often help, there are still ways to execute an SCP article without including a lot of supplements and backstory. In this case, it would be by telling the "story" of the phenomenon that occurs—which is basically what the OP has already done, although the finished article would be longer and more detailed.

That said, in order for an SCP work solely as a description of a phenomenon, it has to be captivating enough to stand on its own, and unfortunately I can't say I'm interested in the concept presented here.

My advice would be to shift your focus from asking "what does it do?" to "what is my theme?" In this case, "international travel is confusing and terrifying" would be a strong thematic avenue to pursue. The Vanishing Hotel Room urban legend, which relies on this theme, has remained in circulation for at least a hundred and seven years.

So how can you tweak your concept to emphasize that theme? One way would be to have people land in a regular foreign city (that doesn't normally have an airport) instead of the wilderness, grappling with language barriers, desperate to find a way home when the way they came doesn't exist anymore. Consider what other emotions and experiences you can add to the mix to give your concept more depth.

item.title: June the 31st
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre (Optional): Emotional

Page Layout (Optional): ACS

Elevator Pitch: This SCP is both the day of June the 31st and the global event that occurs on that day. During the day, members of the public appear to be in a state of complete wholeness and engage in unorthodox, but not unnatural activities. These activities can range from having a picnic in the park, gardening, napping in a graveyard to hugging and weeping. Knowledge of the day appears to be instinctive. People seem to remember it the moment the day begins and steadily forget about it when it finishes1. It also appears that those working for or associated with the Foundation are exempt from this event and are able to remember the happenings of the day. They also don't feel the state of wholeness that the general public experience on the day.

Central Narrative: Something is in the air. Like an uncanny calm. Almost as if the whole world had sighed with relief and tranquility.

The overall story of this SCP is the strange, tranquil state the world enters on June the 31st, the day no-one will remember. Throughout the day, people enter a mindset they will rarely enter on any other day. Everyone is truly occupying their lives. That is, everyone except those in the Foundation, as they appear to be exempt from the SCP's effect. This is further emphasised when Foundation researchers interview people during the SCP. The interviewee treats foundation staff with slight pity and compassion, as if the Foundation is a child who doesn't understand something.

It's suggested that the SCP is necessary in some way. During one experiment, people were subjected to a strong narcotic and skipped the day entirely. Upon waking up, the subject appeared distant, mournful and depressive and continued in this state throughout their lives. It would appear that this SCP maintains a kind of wellbeing inside humanity.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: What I'm really trying to get across is both a feeling of calm peace experienced by the public and a sort of sad envy and exclusion experienced by the Foundation Staff. I haven't seen an SCP which does something beautiful and emphasises the loss Foundation Staff experience when they join the Foundation.

Footnotes
1. This is demonstrated through interviews and experiments.

Does he have a personality and sense of purpose, or is it just effectively a magical robot?

Overall I think you've got an interesting seed of an idea here, but it doesn't sound like it's yet been developed as fully as it needs to be.

item.title: Re: Admin is Asleep, Post Antimemes (Seeking Greenlight)
item.content:encoded:
Overall I think it's a totally viable concept and has the potential for a really great article. I honestly really love the idea of a monster only D-Class can see, with researchers struggling to prove it really exists. My advice is to focus on creating an escalating feeling of paranoia and dread. Avoid "showing" the monster; less is more in articles like this. For instance:

Approximately halfway through the night, Holloway awakens to the sound of rustling papers and the scratches of graphite.

This is wonderfully spooky.

They arise from their bed and see the creature, whom they dub "Admin," watching and presumably writing about Holloway.

This is not.

Greenlight. Good luck!
